$comment: Gold standard for the 6-minute Plaud round of 2026-08-11 (recording a9d4db3d, 370s).
This round is unusual and valuable: the source script (docs/טקסט סבב רופאים.docx)
ends with an author-written validation table of 20 clinical orders, each tagged
with its type and its patient. That table is CLINICAL INTENT authored by a domain
owner — not something reverse-engineered from the model's output — so order recall
is the headline metric here rather than field-level token matching.
THREE-WAY COMPARISON. The script is what was meant; the recording is what the
microphone and speech-to-text actually captured; the note is what the system
produced. The system can only ever work from the recording, so each order carries
an `asrStatus` recording how much of it survived the audio:
full    — the order is fully evidenced in the transcript
partial — the order is present but a clinical detail was lost
lost    — the order is not in the transcript at all; UNACHIEVABLE by any system
That distinction is the point. Without it, an evaluation punishes the system for
transcription damage and the resulting score says nothing about the pipeline.
CEILING: 17 orders full, 2 partial, 1 lost. Maximum achievable order recall is
19/20, and one of those 19 is degraded.

$medicalTermsComment: TERMINOLOGY FIDELITY — a separate axis from order recall.
Order recall asks 'did the instruction arrive'. This asks 'is the clinical
vocabulary right', and the two diverge: an order can reach the chart while the
diagnosis attached to it is a different disease.
Two independent comparisons, because they have different owners:
document -> audio : transcription fidelity. Not the system's doing.
audio -> note     : documentation fidelity. This is what grades the system.
`spokenAs` is what the recording actually contains — null when the term did not
survive at all. `faithful` tokens mean the note recorded what was said (correct,
even when the audio itself was wrong). `inferred` tokens mean the note supplied
clinical vocabulary the audio never contained; that is not automatically wrong —
restoring a mangled spelling is benign — but naming an organ or a disease the
recording never named is a clinical assertion the system invented, and a
